Sunday, two weeks after. Nikita still couldn't say the words 'the shop closed' without her throat tightening. When Tanuja asked, she said, 'I was useless. I did everything wrong.' A minute later: 'Actually, the courier rates went up, it's not my fault.' Both felt true and neither helped.
Wednesday. Tanuja came over with a notebook and drew three columns: in my control, luck, change next time. Nikita filled them slowly. In control: she never raised prices, and she stopped posting new plants in the monsoon. Luck: the courier rates, the heavy rain in August. Change: price for delivery, keep a small stock, check the numbers monthly. She crossed out 'useless'. It didn't fit any column.
The next Saturday she showed the page to her old supplier, who nodded at the price column and said, 'Yes. That was it.' Nikita felt oddly lighter.

qa.q: What three columns did Tanuja draw?
qa.a: She drew three columns: in my control, luck, change next time.

qa.q: Why did Nikita feel 'oddly lighter' on Saturday?
qa.a: She felt relief because seeing the causes clearly turned the failure into something she understood and could fix.

qa.q: What went well in the way Nikita reviewed the closure?
qa.a: She looked fairly at both her own choices and bad luck, instead of either calling herself useless or blaming only the courier.

qa.q: How might Tanuja see the change in Nikita between Sunday and Wednesday?
qa.a: Tanuja may feel glad to see her friend move from swinging between blame and excuses to calm, useful thinking.

grounding: It shows a person, after the first pain eases, sorting what was in her control, what was luck and what to change, turning failure into information.

passage:
Sit down, Eshaan. Your Chinmay Chacha has lost more than one pitch, you know.
When I was twenty-four I failed the state services prelims. I didn't leave my room for three days. Then, for weeks, I swung between two stories. Story one: I'm just not smart enough. Story two: the paper was unfair, the questions changed, bad luck.
My old teacher, Joshi-ma'am, made me write a list. Three questions. What was in my hands? I never did full mock tests with a timer. I read, but I didn't practise. What was luck? Yes, the pattern changed that year. Everyone got the same luck, though. What would I change? Timed tests, every Sunday.
That list was the most useful thing I wrote that whole year, Eshaan. Not because it made me feel better. Because it told me what to do.
So. Your pitch. Get a paper.

qa.q: How many days did Chacha not leave his room after failing the prelims?
qa.a: He didn't leave his room for three days.

qa.q: How did Chacha feel during the weeks he swung between two stories?
qa.a: He felt stuck and discouraged, thinking either he wasn't smart enough or it was all bad luck, and neither story let him move forward.

qa.q: What is Chacha advising Eshaan to do about the lost pitch?
qa.a: He wants Eshaan to write down what was in his hands, what was luck and what to change, so the failure turns into clear next steps.

qa.q: What might Eshaan be feeling as his Chacha tells this story?
qa.a: Eshaan may feel comforted that an elder he respects also failed, and ready to look at the pitch honestly instead of just feeling bad.

grounding: It shows an elder describing an honest review of a failure, separating control, luck and change and avoiding both self-blame and excuses.

passage:
Three weeks after Arnab shut his momo cloud kitchen, the monsoon trapped him and Noor in an auto on a flooded Kolkata street, engine off, water at the footboard. No one was going anywhere for an hour.
"Fine," Arnab said. "Let's do the post-mortem you keep asking for." He pulled out an old menu card and a pen.
Noor drew three columns on the back: in my control, luck, change next time.
In his control: too much spent on fancy boxes, too little testing the recipe with strangers. Two months of ignoring reviews about cold momos.
Luck: the road dug up outside for half the year, a delivery strike in March.
Change: test with twenty real customers first; fix delivery before anything fancy.
"Earlier I'd have said it was all the road," he admitted, "or all me."
Noor tapped the middle column. "Neither. It's a list now."
The water began to drain. Arnab folded the menu and kept it.

qa.q: What did Noor draw on the back of the menu card?
qa.a: Three columns: in my control, luck, change next time.

qa.q: What does Arnab's admission about blaming 'all the road, or all me' suggest about his state now?
qa.a: He feels calmer and more honest, ready to look at causes fairly after weeks of hurt.

qa.q: What is Arnab's most useful change for next time, and why?
qa.a: Testing with twenty real customers first, because it tackles the cold-momo problem he ignored instead of blaming luck.

qa.q: How might Noor feel as the review goes on?
qa.a: Noor is probably relieved and encouraged, seeing Arnab finally willing to look at the failure without excuses or self-blame.

grounding: Stuck in a flood, a young man fairly sorts his failed kitchen into what he controlled, what was luck and what to change.

passage:
A month after the last rejection email, Darshan finally took the festival letters out of the drawer in his Bengaluru flat. Eleven festivals, eleven polite no's for his short film.
Rehana, who had edited it with him, arrived with dosas and a marker. On the fridge whiteboard they wrote two questions: what was ours to control, and what was luck?
Ours: the sound was muddy in the first scene, and they both knew it. The ending ran four minutes too long. They had sent it out without showing it to a single outside viewer.
Luck: two festivals got five thousand entries; one changed its rules after they applied.
Darshan stared at the board. "I kept telling myself either the juries were fools or I'm talentless."
"And now?"
"Now it's three things to fix." Under the list he wrote: clean sound, cut the ending, screen it for ten strangers first.

qa.q: How many festivals rejected Darshan's short film?
qa.a: Eleven festivals, eleven polite no's.

qa.q: What was Darshan feeling when he admitted blaming either the juries or his own talent?
qa.a: He felt relieved and steadier, stepping away from both excuses and self-blame toward a fair view.

qa.q: Which item on the board is most useful, and why?
qa.a: Screening for ten strangers first, since they never had outside viewers and that step would catch problems like muddy sound early.

qa.q: What is it like for Rehana to review the film with Darshan?
qa.a: Rehana shares the failure as the editor, so an honest review is likely a relief, turning a painful month into clear work.

grounding: A young filmmaker separates what was in his control from luck after many rejections and turns the failure into a list of changes.

"You don't have to talk about it yet," Rafiq said.
"No, I want to. It's been two weeks. I'm done crying over it." Jaya pulled her knees up on the sofa. "Ask me the questions. The ones you said."
"Okay. What part was in your control?"
"Honestly? I studied the areas I love and skimmed the statistics. And I never did a mock oral with anyone."
"What was luck?"
"Getting the one examiner who only asks about methods. That was bad luck."
"And what would you change?"
"Two mock orals with seniors. Statistics every morning, not only when I'm scared." She paused. "Two weeks ago I'd have said I'm not cut out for a PhD."
"And now?"
"Now I'd say I prepared badly for one kind of question. That's fixable."
"That's a very different sentence."
"It is." She almost smiled. "Write it down before I forget I said it."

qa.q: What did Jaya skim while studying?
qa.a: The statistics.

qa.q: What does Jaya's almost-smile at the end suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: She feels lighter and more hopeful, now that the failure looks like information rather than proof she is not cut out for a PhD.

qa.q: What makes Jaya's review a fair one?
qa.a: She separates what she controlled, like skimming statistics, from luck like the examiner, and names two concrete changes.

qa.q: How might Rafiq feel as Jaya answers the questions?
qa.a: Rafiq is probably relieved and proud, seeing Jaya look at the failure honestly instead of blaming herself or the examiner.

grounding: After a failed qualifying exam a young woman fairly separates her own choices from luck and decides what to change.

passage: Three months after we shut the café in Bandra, Aparna and I finally sat down with a notebook and the old accounts. In the first weeks after closing, I had swung between two stories: it was all my fault, or it was all the landlord's and the road works' fault. Neither was fair. So we drew three columns. What we controlled: we opened too big, we changed the menu five times, I hired friends I couldn't manage. What was luck: the road dug up for eight months, the rent going up. What to change next time: start smaller, test one menu for a season, hire for skills. Aparna tapped the page and said, "Zubin, look. It's not a verdict. It's a list." It was strangely calming. For the first time, the café felt less like a wound and more like information.

qa.q: What were the three columns?
qa.a: What we controlled, what was luck, and what to change next time.

qa.q: How did the three-column review make Zubin feel?
qa.a: Zubin felt strangely calm, as the café turned from a wound into information.

qa.q: Why was the review better than the two stories Zubin had swung between?
qa.a: It gave a fair look at causes, neither total self-blame nor total excuses, so the failure produced lessons to act on.

qa.q: How does Aparna seem to see the failure?
qa.a: Aparna sees it as a list to learn from, not a verdict on either of them.

grounding: Shows a fair review after a failed venture, sorting what was in their control, what was luck and what to change, turning failure into information.
